title: PCOS Is Now PMOS: Doctors Say the New Name Changes Women's Care
excerpt: The hormonal condition long known as polycystic ovary syndrome has been renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome — a change doctors say should push care beyond period regulation toward metabolic and mental health.
body:
• A hormonal condition affecting one in eight women worldwide has been renamed from polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), in a change published in The Lancet.
  • Doctors say the old name misled patients and clinicians alike: most patients do not have true ovarian cysts, and the condition is a whole-body metabolic and hormonal disorder — not a "period problem."
  • Women with PMOS face a fourfold higher risk of type 2 diabetes and significantly higher risks of heart disease and stroke; they are also three times more likely to experience depression and five times more likely to experience anxiety.
  • Experts urge lifelong, whole-body care — screening for insulin resistance, diabetes and cardiovascular risk, plus mental health support — rather than treatment focused only on regulating menstrual cycles.

One of the most common hormonal conditions in women has a new name — and doctors say the change could reshape how millions of patients are diagnosed and treated. Polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is now polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, shortened to PMOS, following a renaming published in The Lancet after 14 years of collaboration between medical experts and patients. The Endocrine Society, a global group of physicians and scientists, said the old terminology contributed to missed diagnoses and inadequate treatment.

Context & Background

The renaming effort was led by Monash University and drew on more than 22,000 survey responses and 56 patient and professional organisations, according to The Better India. A three-year phase-in is expected, with an updated international guideline due in 2028. Physicians have pushed for the change for years: as far back as 2012, US National Institutes of Health experts wrote that the name focused on a criterion "which is neither necessary nor sufficient to diagnose the syndrome." On ultrasound, what appear to be cysts are typically small, immature follicles — not abnormal cysts at all.

"The thought behind that is that one, there's no cysts in the ovary, so it's very confusing. The hope was that with a more comprehensive and accurate name change, that it would start to enable and push better care."

— Dr. Melanie Cree, pediatric endocrinology expert, University of Colorado Anschutz

The new name is meant to do exactly what it says: polyendocrine (multiple hormone systems), metabolic, ovarian. As gynaecologist Dr. Yash Bahuguna told The Better India, when the name says "metabolic" and "endocrine," doctors are more likely to screen for insulin resistance, diabetes risk, mental health concerns and long-term cardiovascular risk.

Impact & Analysis

Between 50 and 70 percent of women with the condition have insulin resistance and face a fourfold increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes, according to research cited by Florida Atlantic University scientists. The condition is also linked to higher risks of hypertension, cardiovascular disease and stroke — independent of body weight — and long-term studies show nearly a 50 percent increased risk of premature mortality, driven largely by cardiometabolic disease. The mechanism is hormonal: excess insulin drives the ovaries to produce too much testosterone, which causes many of the symptoms, Dr. Cree told the Associated Press.

Mental health is the other half of the story the old name obscured. Women with PMOS are three times more likely to experience depression and up to five times more likely to experience anxiety, the FAU researchers found. Counselling psychologist Damini Grover, writing in The Hindu BusinessLine, described patients carrying "layers of emotional exhaustion" — chronic fatigue, brain fog, mood fluctuations and body-image distress — that are repeatedly minimised. Experts also warn that care must not stop at reproductive age: an FAU review found research on PMOS in midlife largely overlooks chronic pain and mental health, even as symptoms can worsen around menopause.

"This is why long-term care matters, not just period regulation."

— Dr. Yash Bahuguna, gynaecologist, Pinky Promise

Treatment remains personalised: lifestyle change first — less processed food, regular exercise, good sleep — plus metformin or other insulin-sensitising medicines, androgen-blocking drugs or hormonal birth control, depending on symptoms and goals.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian and Indian-origin families, the rename lands in familiar territory: PCOD — an older term for the condition — is still widely used across India, and clinicians say patients often arrive fixated on cysts and periods while the metabolic risks go unscreened. Because South Asian women face elevated baseline risks for diabetes and heart disease, the new name's emphasis on metabolism is especially relevant.

What's Next

The terminology phases in over three years through updated guidelines, medical education and disease classification; the old terms are not becoming invalid overnight. In the meantime, clinicians advise against treating PMOS as a period problem to be managed with a prescription and forgotten — ask about screening for insulin resistance, diabetes and cholesterol, keep up long-term follow-up, and treat mental health as part of the condition.
